## Objectives {#objectives}

By the end of this session you can:

- For a research question, say where the signal shows up and which kind
  of data records it.
- Write down a research idea's data requirements (granularity, frequency,
  where the signal appears) and judge whether a source meets them.
- Classify a data source by access class: open, licensed, restricted or
  self-collected.
- Say what a given source misses about the thing you want to measure.

## What we cover {#coverage}

- The question-to-data map, built from published examples.
  [Henderson, Storeygard & Weil (AER, 2012)](https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.102.2.994)
  measured income growth from night lights (satellite images of light
  given off at night) in countries where official accounts are weak.
  Lights work there as a proxy, a variable you can observe that moves
  with one you cannot.
  [Baker, Bloom & Davis (QJE, 2016)](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjw024)
  counted newspaper articles that mention the economy, policy and
  uncertainty to build a monthly index, and compared the counts with
  human readings of 12,000 articles.
  [Dell & Olken (REStud, 2020)](https://doi.org/10.1093/restud/rdz017)
  digitised handwritten 1850s colonial records of about 10,000 Javanese
  villages forced to grow sugarcane, and matched about 6,400 of them to
  modern locations. Each example starts with its context: a map or
  photo, the dates and the headline numbers.
- The map's legend: text, documents and scans, audio, photographs,
  spatial data and satellite imagery. Much spatial data comes gridded,
  one value per square of a regular net laid over the map for each date.
- Data requirements. The signal is the trace your subject leaves in some
  record. Granularity is the size of the unit the data describe (a
  country, a county, a one-kilometre square), and frequency is how often
  a value is recorded. Name the unit of observation, the thing one row
  describes, and write down where the signal should appear before you
  search. Then verify that the source you pick records it at the
  granularity and frequency you need.
- Access classes, meaning who may obtain a dataset and how. A licence
  sets what you may do with data: use it, share it, publish it or resell
  it. Restricted data can be used only under a signed agreement, often
  on a secure computer, and may not be passed on. Both decide what goes
  into a replication package, the data, code and instructions that let
  someone else rerun your analysis and get the same results.
- What each instrument misses. Coverage is the places, people and years
  a source includes, and measurement error is the gap between what it
  records and the true value. The Java records have a coverage gap:
  about a third of the villages could not be placed on a modern map.
- The formats data ships in (CSV, Excel, Stata, shapefile and others),
  one line each, with the R function that reads it. Read the codebook,
  the document that explains each variable's meaning, units and
  collection, before the data.
